title: Here am I, send me (Isaiah 6)
hookLine: Isaiah sees the Lord, the seraphs cry holy, and a coal touches his lips

lines: HOLY, HOLY, HOLY AT EVERY MASS.
cards: Every Sunday at Mass, just before the Eucharistic Prayer, the whole church sings or says the Sanctus, the song that calls God holy three times over and says heaven and earth are full of his glory. Today, its source.
Now, back before the exile, to the prophets who warned it was coming. One of them is Isaiah, Isaias in the Douay-Rheims.
His book turns on a single moment in the Temple, in the year King Uzziah died, Ozias in the Douay, when a man looks up and sees more than he ever wanted to see.

teach.b: In the Douay: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated: and his train filled the temple." Just the hem of God's robe fills the whole building.
Above him stand seraphim, a name usually taken to mean burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly.
And they call to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house.
And Isaiah's first reaction isn't wonder. It's terror.
"Woe is me," he says, because I am a man of unclean lips, living among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King.

Then one of the seraphim flies to him holding a live coal, taken with tongs from the altar, and touches his mouth with it: thy iniquities shall be taken away, and thy sin shall be cleansed. Not punishment. Cleansing.
Only then does God speak, almost to himself: "Whom shall I send? and who shall go for us?"

teach.h: LO, HERE AM I, SEND ME.
teach.b: And Isaiah answers: "Lo, here am I, send me." In Hebrew, here am I is a single word, hineni. Abraham says it.
Moses says it at the bush. The boy Samuel says it in the night. It means I'm present, I'm listening, use me.

The seraphim's cry became the Sanctus at every Mass. And in the older form of the Mass, the priest prays before reading the Gospel that God would cleanse his lips as he cleansed the lips of Isaiah with a burning coal.

how: At every Mass, Catholics sing or say the Sanctus, Holy, holy, holy, drawn from the seraphim's cry in Isaiah 6, and the call of Isaiah is often read at ordinations and on Sundays about vocation.

o: woe is me: a cry of being undone
holy, holy, holy: the angels' song
here I am: present, listening, ready

games.q: in the Temple — tap the pairs.
p: the seraphim's cry, now the Sanctus

s: Isaiah volunteered the moment he saw the Lord
his first words were woe is me. he spoke up only after the coal cleansed his lips.
the Sanctus at Mass comes from this vision
Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts: the seraphim's cry.
the coal was a punishment for Isaiah's sin
it cleansed him: thy iniquities shall be taken away.

games.q: you're Isaiah. you've seen the Lord, your lips have just been touched with a burning coal, and you hear: whom shall I send? what do you say?
o: nothing; it wasn't said to you.
games.why: Isaiah answers: lo, here am I, send me. the same man who said woe is me a moment before.

practice: Think of one thing that needs doing that nobody has volunteered for: the dishes nobody claims, the hard phone call, the meal for a family with a new baby.
If something in you says woe is me, I'm not the right person, Isaiah said that too; quietly say his words about that one task, here am I, send me, and if you pray, say them to God.

wordCard.voice: hineni. Hebrew for here I am: present, listening, ready, Isaiah's answer after the coal touched his lips. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: here I am, one word. Said by Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah when God calls.

carryVoice: Your line: whom shall I send. A cleansed mouth, and a ready answer. Day four hundred fifteen, done.
